title: Java4Shell: RCE in OpenJDK when processing Base64 (calif.io)
comments: From the section on performing heap grooming over the network ("Remote Heap Feng Shui"):> The current attack is sensitive to network conditions, like RTT and jitter. Low, stable round-trip times are preferred for a more reliable attack. In our controlled environment, we performed this attack over the internet through public IP addresses instead of just assuming perfect laboratory conditions. For the current attack path to achieve optimal stability and reliability in exploitation, Calif turned to physics and utilized money to solve the problem, rather than experimenting with TCP/IP stack configuration. In other words, Calif rented another VM in the same region as our target.And the "Limitations" section:> There is no universal payload. Each chain needs a decoder route, a live writer, a returned reader or another feedback path, a heap layout, and an application action. Every target needs a bespoke profile. The exploit is not a universal point-and-shoot.Based on the complexity and constraints, short-term mass-exploitation seems unlikely. It will take some time before there are reliable exploits, and they may require running on infra close to the target.But a long tail of unpatched java applications/services at high-value targets getting exploited, seems plausible to me.reply

title: GPT‑6.2 Astra and Sol (openai.com)
comments: Pretty incredible cost reductions. In our data analytics exam [1], Astra went from ~$20 (V6) to ~$4 (V6.2) and Sol went from $2.6 (V6.1) to $1.2 (V6.2).Similar accuracy in both. It's cheaper both because of token reduction (20%) but it also took less tool calls to answer the questions. In some cases, it "finished early" and didn't find the answer we were looking for.Also very fast. Both Astra & Sol are the 2 fastest models I've tested that got at least an A in the exam.[1] https://plotly.com/blog/gpt-6-2-sol-plotly-data-analytics-be...reply
I’m curious if people think the cost reductions are legitimately because the new model uses less resources, or if people think they are playing subsidization games to hype new models.reply

It is impossible to say for sure, but I think there is a very high chance these models do in fact run more efficiently:* We can see in the Chinese open weight models that there has been a clear trend of moving to more efficient hybrid attention formats over the last year (see e.g. https://sebastianraschka.com/blog/2026/full-to-hybrid-attent...), and presumably the closed labs have been following a similar path, perhaps using the innovations the Chinese labs are using, or perhaps developing their own. And at this point the models themselves are good enough to accelerate developing all sorts of efficiency improvements which can then be used in the next generation.* The most dramatic pricing cuts are often on cached read tokens, which suggests KV cache efficiency improvements. Other token types haven't had pricing cut so much. If this was just a subsidy they'd probably have cut pricing more evenly across the board.Finally, I do not think it is in the interests of the big labs to slash their margins on inference for api (i.e. enterprise) pricing. Much of their high value comes from having very big margins on inference (and we now know for sure that they do have them, see Anthropic's S1). There is presumably a strong shared desire to not have a race down to commodity margins. So most likely if they are cutting prices, their cost of inference has fallen. Individual subscriptions are a totally different matter, they are heavily subsidized compared to api pricing, and those are indeed about generating hype and developer mindshare. But they are not where the labs are getting their revenue.reply

I believe they're optimizations, but they're at the point where they reduce performance elsewhere. They lost points on some benchmarks here.All the LLMs have dropped significantly in writing quality, to the point that YC even created a RFS and everyone started using ASD-STE100. Claude was incomprehensible because it was using token-dense terminology.reply
> All the LLMs have dropped significantly in writing quality,I think it's an intended consequence of RL on long-term tasks, where most of LLM writing targets itselfreply

The provenance statements are more or less a capture of the moment and the LLM tends to rebuild the scenario around that. It’s absolutely possible to structure how the agent responds and records data. I made stylistic guidelines regarding how agents express and record information in their tickets. It makes for a cleaner presentation of work and focuses the agent. This was entirely a reaction to opuses earlier behavior, but long term the work has paid dividends.reply
Not intended, but yes a natural evolutionary result of RLVR training.reply
Providers sell you GPU-hours and utilization. Tokens, subscriptions, and your data are just ways to price it, unrelated to actual costs.reply
Inference has been ~80-90% margin. It’s more showing how overpriced API pricing has been all along.reply
Isn’t the point to recoup the cost of training? Like, inference is insanely profitable if you didn’t need to park 70% of your GPUs doing training for weeks.reply

title: Why Fibonacci? (evilgeniuslabs.org)

first_paragraph:
I was inspired to create my first Fibonacci LED piece after seeing this video by Jim Bumgardner in 2015. I credit him for starting my Fibonacci obsession.Fast forward to 2026. I’ve made dozens of Fibonacci designs. Recently, I saw this brilliant post by Nick Pisarro explaining the use of the golden angle in creating his beautiful Halo Pixel. It got me thinking about how to explain the techniques I use.Every Fibonacci board I make, from the tiny One Inch Fibonacci64 to the Fibonacci1024, puts its LEDs on a Fermat spiral, the same pattern as the seeds in a sunflower. It’s different from the “Fibonacci spiral” drawn from squares, which is a single curve. The Fibonacci step shows where the name comes from.Start at the center. Then repeat:Every LED on every¹ Fibonacci board is placed by those rules. LED n sits n × 137.508° around from the first, and about √n out from the center. The next two steps explain those two numbers.
¹ There are exceptions to the √n rule, of course, like Fibonacci64

title: 350 years ago, Ole Rømer discovered that light has a finite speed (sciencenorway.no)
comments: I created a web comic based on this measurement! https://randomlyunique.com/plancky/2018/roemers-speed-of-lig...reply

From the comic: "Over the course of a year, Io's orbital time varied by 22 minutes".This sentence implies that at some point in the year the time it takes for Io to do one single orbit, as viewed from earth is 22 minutes longer. That's not true. This is not a good explanation comic.What happens is that if you have a clock that is very accurate and has a drift of less than a minute for a whole year, and you measure the exact moment that Io's eclipse happens (every 42.5 hours) over a full year, you might expect that it's every 42.5 hours all the way through the year. But what you actually see is that this moment varies over the course of a year by 22 minutes - it's later if Jupiter is far away.Now you might ask how can somebody create such an accurate clock - in the 17th century? He used a pendulum clock which had a drift of like a second in 6 hours, and at the beginning of each night, he corrected that clock based on some other daily occurring measurement of the night sky, like when a certain star crosses a fixed point when viewed from his observatory.reply

Oof, "not a good explanation comic" is a bit harsh. I deliberately skipped the synodic-period / cumulative-delay framing because I worried it would add a layer of complexity that might bog down a comic aimed at people with zero physics background.reply

I didn't write the original comment but perhaps a suggestion that may satisfy both of you would be to say the "apparent orbital time"? Except the explanation doesn't make any sense. A period is a period.
Earth doesn't look like its spinning half as fast if you are 1 light-day away...The real effect is actually to do with making a graph and noticing an oscillation in the phase of the orbit. In particular the cumulative phase shifts that add up as earth moves further away and the cumulative small phase shifts that add up as earth moves closer to Jupiter. This looks like a sine wave.Like if someone before you made a table of predicated date and times of io transits (Cassini's constant-period tables) based on the assumption that the oscillation is jitter-free, you could actually realize that there is this +-11 minute jitter in the real measurements after collecting a lot of samples.There are lots of these textbook simplifications that make a line fitting problem look like some magic 2 point measurement impossibility.Like the Millikan’s oil drop experiment wasn't some magic nonsense where you figure out how to balance a single drop in mid air.The Cavendish weighing the earth wasn't a static twist on some wire where you cannot possibly measure the torsion constant precisely enough. It involved measuring a peak to peak deflection of some small oscillation.The Foucault rotating mirror was not magically shooting a discrete laser pulse and measuring an RPM, as it came back in the second gap it was realising that you could modulate the returning intensity as you ramped angular frequency. Fitting angular velocity against harmonic number was what gives you time of flight not a single tooth.reply
